options: Converting a log file from one storage format to another with no change in content structure
A step that only applies to logs collected via syslog, never Windows logs
Extracting structured, named fields — like source IP, username, and event type — out of raw unstructured log text
Deleting log entries that are no longer needed
questions.explain: Parsing turns raw text into structured fields the SIEM can filter, sort, and compare on.

questions.q: Before a raw syslog line is parsed, how does the SIEM treat it?
options: As an unstructured string, searchable only by exact substring until a parser extracts fields from it
Unparsed lines are automatically converted to CEF format
As a set of fully structured fields from the moment it arrives
The SIEM cannot store unparsed log lines at all
questions.explain: Until a parser runs, a raw log line is just text — meaningful to a human reading it, but not yet structured for the SIEM to search on by field.

questions.q: Why does field extraction matter beyond just making search more convenient?
options: It has no real purpose beyond making text easier to read
It only matters for compliance reporting, not for detection
It's the prerequisite for correlation rules, which compare field values across different log sources
It replaces the need for log storage entirely
questions.explain: Correlation rules compare parsed field values across sources, such as the same src_ip appearing in two different events — something impossible on unparsed text.

questions.q: What is normalization in the context of log parsing?
options: Mapping differently-named fields from different sources (src_ip, SourceAddress, sourceIPAddress) into one common field name
Removing duplicate log entries from the same source
Compressing log files to save storage space
Converting all logs into the syslog protocol regardless of origin
questions.explain: Normalization resolves the fact that different sources name the same concept differently, mapping them to one shared field the whole platform uses.

questions.q: What real risk does a lack of normalization create for a correlation rule?
options: Normalization has no effect on correlation rules
The SIEM would refuse to ingest unnormalized logs
The rule would run faster without normalization
The rule could quietly miss events where the same data was logged under a different field name
questions.explain: A rule written against a specific field name, like src_ip, misses matching data logged under a differently named field from another source.
